blogPosts.title: Employee Retention: Why People Stay and How to Keep Them
blogPosts.excerpt: Replacing good employees is expensive. Learn what keeps people engaged and the simple habits that reduce turnover.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-team-briefing.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table

children.text: Every resignation costs more than a recruitment fee. Teams lose knowledge, projects slow down and colleagues take on extra work. Most people do not leave for salary alone; they leave when they stop growing or feeling valued. To keep your best people, focus on these three areas:
Understand Why People Stay
1. Hold Regular Stay Interviews
Ask employees what keeps them here and what might tempt them away, long before they start considering offers from other companies.
2. Show Clear Career Paths
Explain how promotions work and which skills each next step requires, so ambitious people can see their future inside your company.
3. Recognize Good Work Often
Specific, timely thanks from managers and peers costs little, yet it strongly influences whether people feel their contribution truly matters.

gallery: blog-team-standup.webp::Three team members talking during a stand-up meeting
blog-candidate-conversation.webp::Hiring manager in conversation with a candidate during an interview

children.text: Why Managers Make or Break Retention

People often leave managers rather than companies. Train team leaders to give useful feedback, discuss development goals regularly and notice early signs of burnout, because these everyday conversations shape how employees feel about their work.
Offer Flexibility and Fair Rewards

Competitive pay matters, but so does the way work fits into people's lives. Review salaries against the market every year, and offer flexible hours or hybrid options where the role allows, so employees do not need to leave to find balance.
Use exit interviews to learn from every departure as well. Look for patterns across teams and managers, then act on what you hear, so the same reasons do not cause the next resignation.

image.$media: blog-inline-hr-paperwork.webp::HR specialist handing over a stack of files to a colleague

children.text: What Better Retention Delivers
Lower Turnover Costs
– Fewer resignations mean less spending on recruitment, onboarding and training for replacement hires.
Stronger Teams
– Experienced employees share knowledge, mentor newcomers and keep projects moving without constant handovers.
Happier Customers
– Long-serving staff build lasting relationships that customers notice, value and reward with their loyalty.

blogPosts.title: Inclusive Hiring: Practical Steps to Build Diverse Teams
blogPosts.excerpt: Diverse teams make better decisions. Practical ways to remove bias from hiring and welcome a wider range of talent.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-interview-tips.webp::Hiring manager and candidate talking during an interview

children.text: Talented people come from every background, yet many hiring processes quietly favor candidates who look, speak and think like the existing team. Inclusive hiring is not about lowering standards; it is about removing barriers that hide great candidates. Start with these three practical changes:
Remove Bias at Every Stage
1. Focus on Skills, Not Pedigree
Assess what candidates can actually do instead of where they studied or worked, and drop degree requirements that the role does not need.
2. Use Diverse Interview Panels
Include interviewers with different backgrounds and roles, so decisions reflect more than one point of view and candidates feel genuinely welcome.
3. Make Your Process Accessible
Offer flexible interview times, accessible locations and reasonable adjustments, and tell every candidate clearly how to request the support they need.

gallery: blog-colleagues-discussion.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet
blog-mentoring-desk.webp::Team lead mentoring a new hire at her computer

children.text: Why Sourcing Determines Who Applies

If every hire comes from the same few channels, your shortlist will always look the same. Partner with community groups, specialist job boards and returner programs to reach talented people your usual sources never find.
Measure Progress Openly

Track who applies, who is shortlisted and who receives offers at each stage, using anonymous data collected with consent. Patterns in these numbers show where candidates from underrepresented groups drop out, so you can fix the specific step responsible.

Share your goals and progress with employees and candidates. Transparency builds trust, invites useful feedback and shows that your commitment to inclusion goes further than a statement on your careers page.

image.$media: blog-inline-team-briefing.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table

children.text: What Inclusive Hiring Delivers
Wider Talent Pool
– Removing unnecessary barriers brings skilled candidates into your process who would otherwise never have applied.
Better Decisions
– Teams with different experiences challenge assumptions and find stronger solutions to complex business problems.
Stronger Reputation
– Candidates and customers increasingly choose companies that treat people fairly and reflect the communities they serve.

blogPosts.title: Your Next Career Move: How to Prepare for a Job Search
blogPosts.excerpt: A focused job search saves time and leads to better offers. Practical steps to prepare before you apply anywhere.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-advisor-meeting.webp::Advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table

children.text: Searching for a new job can feel like a full-time job in itself. Sending dozens of identical applications rarely works, and it quickly drains your motivation. A little preparation makes every application stronger and every interview easier. Before you apply for your next role, work through these steps:
Prepare Before You Apply
1. Clarify What You Want
Decide which roles, industries, salary range and working style suit you best, so you only spend time on opportunities that genuinely fit.
2. Update Your Resume and Profile
Highlight measurable achievements instead of duties, keep the layout simple, and make sure your online profile tells the same clear story.
3. Tailor Every Application
Match your resume and cover letter to the language of each job description, showing exactly how your experience meets the employer's needs.

gallery: blog-team-briefing.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table
blog-hr-paperwork.webp::HR specialist handing over a stack of files to a colleague

children.text: Why Your Network Opens Hidden Opportunities

Many roles are filled through referrals before they are ever advertised. Reconnect with former colleagues, attend industry events and let trusted contacts know what you are looking for, because a warm introduction often reaches a hiring manager faster.
Get Ready for Every Interview

Research the company's products, recent news and culture before each interview. Prepare short stories that show how you solved problems, worked in a team and delivered results, and practice telling each one clearly in two minutes or less.
Write down thoughtful questions about the team, its goals and the expectations for your first months. Good questions show genuine interest and help you decide whether the role is truly right for you.

image.$media: blog-inline-colleagues-discussion.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet

children.text: What a Focused Job Search Delivers
Better Matches
– You apply for roles that fit your skills and goals, so interviews feel natural and offers become more likely.
Less Stress
– A clear plan replaces endless scrolling and gives you more energy for the applications that really matter.
Stronger Offers
– Well-prepared candidates negotiate with confidence because they understand their value and the market.

blogPosts.title: Talent Acquisition for Growing Businesses
blogPosts.excerpt: Growing companies cannot afford slow or random hiring. Build a talent acquisition approach that scales with your business.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-talent-acquisition-hero.webp::Consultant presenting hiring analytics on a large screen to two colleagues

children.text: When a business grows quickly, hiring often becomes a series of urgent requests handled one at a time. Founders interview between meetings, job ads are written in a hurry and great candidates slip away. A simple talent acquisition strategy changes that. Start with these essentials:
Set Your Hiring Foundations
1. Define Your Hiring Priorities
Identify the roles that unlock the most growth over the next twelve months, and fill those first instead of reacting to every request.
2. Create a Repeatable Process
Use the same steps, interview questions and scorecards for each role, so every hiring manager follows one clear and fair process.
3. Set a Realistic Hiring Budget
Plan salaries, job board costs, agency fees and onboarding expenses together, so growth hiring never surprises your finance team or delays important launches.

gallery: blog-colleagues-discussion.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet
blog-mentoring-desk.webp::Team lead mentoring a new hire at her computer

children.text: Why Regular Reviews Keep Hiring on Track

Talent acquisition is never finished. Review your hiring data every quarter to see which sources bring hires who stay, how long each stage takes and where candidates drop out, then adjust before small problems grow.
Choose the Right Sourcing Channels

Not every channel works for every role. Specialist job boards suit technical positions, referrals often bring strong cultural fits and a recruitment partner can fill senior or urgent roles quickly. Track each channel and invest more in the ones that consistently perform best.

Build relationships with promising candidates even when you are not hiring. Regular, friendly updates keep your company in their minds, so the next time a role opens you already have people ready to talk.

image.$media: blog-inline-advisor-meeting.webp::Recruitment advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table

children.text: Key Benefits for Growing Teams
Predictable Growth
– Planned hiring means new teams are in place before demand peaks, not months after it arrives.
Better-Quality Hires
– Consistent assessments help you choose people who succeed in the role and stay for the long term.
Lower Cost per Hire
– Focusing on proven channels reduces wasted ad spend and expensive last-minute agency placements.

blogPosts.title: Reducing Time to Hire Without Lowering the Bar
blogPosts.excerpt: Top candidates are off the market within weeks. Learn how to shorten your hiring process while keeping quality high.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-hiring-analytics.webp::Two colleagues reviewing reports at a desk

children.text: The strongest candidates often accept another offer while your team is still scheduling interviews. A slow process costs you talent, adds pressure on existing staff and delays important projects. The good news is that speed and quality can work together. Begin with these changes:
Remove Delays from Your Process
1. Measure Every Hiring Stage
Track how many days candidates spend at each step, from application to offer, so you can see exactly where time is lost.
2. Book Interviews in Advance
Reserve interview slots in hiring managers' calendars before a role opens, so shortlisted candidates can be invited within a day or two.
3. Cut Unnecessary Interview Rounds
Combine overlapping conversations into a single panel interview, and remove any step that never changes the final hiring decision.

gallery: blog-advisor-meeting.webp::Recruitment advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table
blog-team-standup.webp::Three team members talking during a stand-up meeting

children.text: Why Fast Feedback Keeps Candidates Engaged

Silence is one of the main reasons candidates withdraw. Commit to giving feedback within two working days after every interview, and keep applicants informed about the next step, even when there is no news to share yet.
Build Talent Pipelines Before You Need Them

The fastest hires are often people you already know. Stay in touch with strong runner-up candidates, encourage employee referrals and maintain a talent pool for your most common roles, so you can start conversations the same day a vacancy opens.

Prepare approved job descriptions, interview questions and scoring guides for recurring positions as well. When the paperwork is ready in advance, recruiters can focus on finding and persuading the best people.

image.$media: blog-inline-candidate-conversation.webp::Hiring manager in conversation with a candidate during an interview

children.text: What a Faster Process Delivers
Higher Offer Acceptance
– Candidates accept more often when they feel wanted and do not wait weeks for a decision.
Lower Hiring Costs
– Shorter vacancies reduce overtime, temporary staffing costs and lost productivity across the business.
Better Candidate Experience
– A quick, well-organized process leaves a positive impression on every applicant, including those you decline.

blogPosts.title: Writing Job Descriptions That Attract the Right Talent
blogPosts.excerpt: Your job ad is a sales pitch. Write job descriptions that attract qualified candidates and filter out poor matches.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-focused-work-desk.webp::Professional working focused at a desk with a monitor and lamp

children.text: A job description is often the first conversation you have with a future employee. Yet many ads are long lists of requirements copied from older postings, and strong candidates skim them and move on. To write ads that people actually read and act on, focus on three things:
Write for the Candidate
1. Use a Clear, Searchable Job Title
Choose the title candidates actually search for and avoid internal jargon, so your role appears in results and is understood at a glance.
2. Lead with the Impact of the Role
Explain what the person will achieve in their first year and why it matters, before listing daily tasks or required skills.
3. Separate Must-Haves from Nice-to-Haves
Keep essential requirements short and realistic, because long wish lists discourage capable people, especially those who apply only when they meet every point.

gallery: blog-hr-paperwork.webp::HR specialist handing over a stack of files to a colleague
blog-team-briefing.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table

children.text: Why Salary Ranges Build Trust

Candidates want to know whether a role fits their expectations before investing time in an application. Publishing a fair salary range attracts more serious applicants, shortens negotiations and shows that your company values openness from the first step.
Use Inclusive, Plain Language

Short sentences and everyday words make your ad easier to read on a phone and easier to understand for non-native speakers. Avoid gendered terms, unnecessary acronyms and buzzwords like “rockstar” or “ninja” that quietly discourage many qualified people from applying.
Before publishing, ask a team member in a similar role to read the ad. If they recognize their real job in it, candidates will too, and the people who apply will arrive with accurate expectations.

image.$media: blog-inline-team-presentation.webp::Consultant presenting hiring analytics on a screen to two colleagues

children.text: What Better Job Descriptions Deliver
More Qualified Applicants
– Clear requirements attract people who match the role and discourage applications that waste everyone's time.
Faster Screening
– Recruiters review fewer unsuitable profiles, so shortlists are ready sooner and interviews can start earlier.
Stronger First Impressions
– A clear, honest ad shows candidates that your company is organized, respectful and worth joining.

blogPosts.title: Structured Interviews: Fairer Decisions and Better Hires
blogPosts.excerpt: Unstructured interviews reward confidence, not ability. See how structured interviews help you compare candidates fairly and hire well.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-candidate-conversation.webp::Hiring manager in conversation with a candidate during an interview

children.text: Many hiring decisions still rest on a pleasant conversation and a gut feeling. The result is inconsistent choices, missed talent and hires who struggle once they start. Structured interviews give every candidate the same fair chance to show what they can do. Here is how to begin:
Build Your Interview Framework
1. Start with the Job Requirements
List the skills and behaviors that truly predict success in the role, and design every question to test one of them directly.
2. Ask Every Candidate the Same Questions
Use the same core questions in the same order, so answers can be compared fairly instead of depending on how the conversation flows.
3. Score Answers with a Rubric
Define what poor, good and excellent answers look like before interviews start, and score each response independently right after the conversation.

gallery: blog-advisor-meeting.webp::Recruitment advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table
blog-team-standup.webp::Three team members talking during a stand-up meeting

children.text: Why Interviewer Training Makes the Difference

Even the best question set fails if interviewers improvise. Short training sessions teach hiring managers to follow the structure, take useful notes, avoid leading questions and recognize their own biases before they influence a decision.
Combine Interviews with Practical Tasks

Interviews show how candidates talk about their work, while practical tasks show how they actually do it. A short, time-limited exercise that mirrors real responsibilities gives you clear evidence and helps candidates understand the role better.

Bring the interview panel together after every final round to compare scores and evidence. Discussing ratings openly, rather than sharing general impressions, leads to faster agreement and decisions you can explain to anyone.

image.$media: blog-inline-mentoring-desk.webp::Team lead mentoring a new hire at her computer

children.text: What Structured Interviews Deliver
Fairer Hiring
– Every candidate is assessed against the same criteria, which reduces bias and widens your talent pool.
Better Predictions
– Scores based on job-related evidence predict on-the-job performance far better than gut feeling alone.
Faster Decisions
– Clear rubrics and shared notes help hiring panels agree quickly and move strong candidates to an offer.

blogPosts.title: Employer Branding: Why Top Candidates Choose You
blogPosts.excerpt: Great candidates research employers before they apply. Learn how to build an employer brand that attracts the right people.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-colleagues-discussion.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet

children.text: Before they apply, most candidates read reviews, browse your careers page and ask friends what working for you is really like. Your employer brand is already being formed, whether you manage it or not. To shape it with intention, start with these three foundations:
Define What Makes You Different
1. Ask Your Employees First
Run short surveys and interviews to learn why people joined, why they stay and what they would honestly change about working here.
2. Write a Clear Value Proposition
Summarize what you offer beyond salary, such as growth, flexibility, purpose and culture, in a few sentences any candidate can understand.
3. Keep Every Message Consistent
Use the same promises on your careers page, job ads, social channels and interviews, so candidates hear one believable story.

gallery: blog-team-briefing.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table
blog-candidate-conversation.webp::Hiring manager in conversation with a candidate during an interview

children.text: Why Authentic Stories Beat Polished Slogans

Candidates trust real people more than marketing copy. Short employee stories, honest team photos and day-in-the-life videos show what work actually feels like, and they attract applicants who will genuinely enjoy your culture and stay.
Turn Your Careers Page Into a Hiring Tool

Your careers page is often the first place a candidate meets your brand. Show open roles clearly, include salary ranges where possible, explain the hiring steps and answer common questions, so qualified people feel confident enough to apply.

Measure what works by tracking page visits, application rates and the sources of your best hires. Small improvements to headlines, photos and calls to action can noticeably lift the number of qualified applicants.

image.$media: blog-inline-team-presentation-2.webp::Consultant presenting hiring analytics on a screen to two colleagues

children.text: What a Strong Employer Brand Delivers
Better Applicants
– Candidates who share your values apply more often, so recruiters spend less time screening unsuitable profiles.
Lower Hiring Costs
– A trusted reputation reduces your reliance on paid job ads and agency fees for hard-to-fill roles.
Higher Retention
– People who join with realistic expectations settle in faster and stay with your company much longer.

blogPosts.title: Hiring Across Time Zones: A Guide to Remote Recruitment
blogPosts.excerpt: Remote hiring widens your talent pool. Learn how to source, interview and onboard great people wherever they live.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-team-standup.webp::Three team members talking during a stand-up meeting

children.text: Remote work has turned local vacancies into global opportunities. You can now hire the best person for a role instead of the best person within commuting distance. But distributed hiring brings its own challenges. Before you open your next remote role, get these basics right:
Set Up a Remote-Ready Process
1. Define Working Hours Clearly
State the core hours and time zones each role must overlap with, so candidates can judge honestly whether the schedule suits their life.
2. Use Asynchronous Assessments
Short written tasks and recorded answers let candidates in any time zone show their skills without late-night or early-morning interviews.
3. Check Local Employment Rules
Contracts, payroll, taxes and benefits differ between countries, so confirm the right hiring model before you make an offer to an international candidate.

gallery: blog-advisor-meeting.webp::Recruitment advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table
blog-hr-paperwork.webp::HR specialist handing over a stack of files to a colleague

children.text: Why Communication Skills Matter Even More

In a remote team, most collaboration happens in writing. Assess how clearly candidates explain ideas, give updates and ask questions, because strong written communication often predicts remote success better than years of experience alone.
Run Video Interviews That Feel Personal

Send each candidate the agenda, interviewer names and meeting link in advance, and test your own setup before the call. Start with a few minutes of informal conversation, then follow the same structured questions you would use in person.

Close every interview by explaining the next steps and timeline. Remote candidates cannot read the atmosphere of an office, so clear and timely communication is what makes them feel valued and respected.

image.$media: blog-inline-colleagues-discussion-2.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet

children.text: What Remote Hiring Delivers
Wider Talent Pool
– You reach skilled candidates in new cities and countries instead of competing for the same local applicants.
Faster Hiring
– Flexible, asynchronous steps remove the scheduling delays that usually stretch interviews across several weeks.
More Diverse Teams
– People with different backgrounds and perspectives bring fresh ideas that help your business solve problems better.

blogPosts.title: Onboarding That Works: Making the First 90 Days Count
blogPosts.excerpt: New hires decide early whether to stay. Plan the first 90 days so people feel welcome, prepared and productive.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-mentoring-desk.webp::Team lead guiding a colleague through an interface on her computer

children.text: Hiring the right person is only half the job. Many new employees leave within their first few months, often because their first weeks felt confusing or lonely. A structured onboarding plan prevents that. Build yours around these three practical stages:
Plan the First Three Months
1. Prepare Before Day One
Send a welcome note, set up equipment and accounts, and share a simple first-week schedule, so the new hire arrives confident instead of anxious.
2. Set Clear 30-60-90 Day Goals
Agree on realistic milestones for each month, so the new hire knows what success looks like and their manager can measure progress fairly.
3. Assign an Onboarding Buddy
Pair every newcomer with a friendly colleague outside their reporting line who can answer everyday questions and introduce them to the wider team.

gallery: blog-candidate-conversation.webp::Hiring manager in conversation with a candidate during an interview
blog-team-standup.webp::Three team members talking during a stand-up meeting

children.text: Why Manager Check-Ins Matter Most

The manager shapes the new hire experience more than any handbook. Short weekly check-ins during the first three months catch problems early, clarify priorities and show new employees that their progress genuinely matters to the business.
Make Culture Part of Onboarding

Policies and paperwork are necessary, but they rarely make people feel they belong. Explain how decisions are made, introduce the people behind each team and share the stories behind your values, so newcomers understand how work really gets done.
Ask every new hire for feedback at 30 and 90 days. Their fresh perspective reveals gaps in your process, outdated documents and confusing steps that long-serving employees simply no longer notice.

image.$media: blog-inline-team-briefing-2.webp::Manager briefing a team seated around a conference table

children.text: What Great Onboarding Delivers
Faster Productivity
– New hires contribute sooner because they know their goals, tools and contacts from the very first week.
Higher Retention
– Employees who feel welcomed and supported are far more likely to stay beyond their first year.
Stronger Engagement
– Clear expectations and regular feedback build the confidence and trust that keep people motivated over time.

blogPosts.title: Workforce Planning: Building Teams That Scale
blogPosts.excerpt: Reactive hiring costs time and money. Learn how to forecast talent needs and build teams that grow with you.
blogPosts.mainImage: blog-hr-paperwork.webp::Specialist handing a stack of project files to a colleague

children.text: Most companies start hiring only when someone resigns or a team is already overloaded. By then, every vacancy feels urgent and every decision is rushed. Workforce planning replaces that cycle with a clear view of the skills you need next. Start with these three steps:
Map Your Talent Needs
1. Audit the Skills You Have
List the skills, experience and certifications across every team, so you can spot strengths, single points of failure and gaps before they cause problems.
2. Link Hiring to Business Goals
Translate next year's revenue targets, product launches and new markets into the roles, headcount and timing each plan will realistically require.
3. Plan for Several Scenarios
Prepare hiring plans for steady, fast and slow growth, so you can act quickly instead of starting from scratch when conditions change.

gallery: blog-colleagues-discussion.webp::Three colleagues discussing plans around a tablet
blog-mentoring-desk.webp::Team lead mentoring a new hire at her computer

children.text: Why Internal Mobility Belongs in Your Plan

Not every gap needs an external hire. Promoting and retraining existing employees is often faster and cheaper, keeps valuable knowledge in the business, and shows your people that ambition and growth are genuinely rewarded here.
Review Your Plan Every Quarter

A workforce plan is only useful while it reflects reality. Review it every quarter with finance and department heads, compare planned headcount with actual hires and attrition, and adjust priorities before small differences turn into missed targets or overstretched teams.

Share the updated plan with recruiters early, so they can build candidate pipelines months before a role opens. Proactive sourcing shortens time to hire and gives you a stronger choice of candidates when budgets are approved.

image.$media: blog-inline-advisor-meeting-2.webp::Recruitment advisor reviewing documents with a client at a bright office table

children.text: What Good Workforce Planning Delivers
Predictable Hiring Costs
– Budgets are set in advance, so fewer roles are filled in a rush through expensive emergency channels.
Stronger Teams
– The right skills arrive before projects start, so teams deliver on time without burning out their best people.
Faster Growth
– New markets, products and offices launch on schedule because the people behind them are already in place.

jobs.title: Market Analyst

Collect and clean sales, pricing and competitor data from many sources.
Build dashboards and monthly reports that track category and menu trends.
Analyze guest surveys and segment customers by visit behavior and value.
Present findings to leadership and help shape pricing and location decisions.
Keep research notes and data sources organized and current.
1-3 years in market research or business analysis
Strong Excel or Google Sheets skills, including pivot tables
Working knowledge of SQL and Looker or Power BI
Confidence explaining numbers in simple language
Degree in economics, statistics or business
Experience with Python or R for analysis
Background in restaurants, retail or hospitality
Familiarity with survey platforms and sampling
Experience with location or footfall data
Competitive salary with a yearly bonus
Hybrid schedule in downtown Chicago
Yearly learning budget for courses
Health insurance from day one
Small team where analysis drives decisions

jobs.shortSummary: Orbitly Apps needs a Mid-Level UI/UX Designer to shape web and mobile products, from early research to polished, developer-ready screens.

You will own features end to end, from user interviews and flows to prototypes and clean, documented files for engineers.
Turn product requirements into user flows, wireframes and high-fidelity screens.
Run quick usability tests and feed results back into the design.
Maintain and extend client design systems in Figma.
Work with developers during the build to keep the product true to design.
Present design decisions clearly to clients and the wider product team.
2-4 years of experience designing digital products
A portfolio showing shipped work and thinking
Advanced Figma skills, including variables and auto layout
Solid understanding of accessibility and responsive design
Comfortable working async across time zones
Experience with motion design or micro-interactions
Basic knowledge of HTML and CSS
Background in SaaS dashboards or health-tech
Experience mentoring junior designers
Fully remote role with flexible hours
Home office setup allowance
Four-day week every other Friday
Paid conferences and design tools
Team that reviews work kindly

jobs.title: UI/UX Designer
jobs.shortSummary: Quantra Software is hiring a UI/UX Designer to design clear, accessible screens for its customer platform, working closely with product and engineering.

children.text: Quantra Software builds a customer platform used daily by small businesses and is looking for a thoughtful UI/UX Designer.
You will work with a product manager and four engineers to research, design and ship new features in every sprint.
Design user flows, wireframes and polished interfaces for web and mobile.
Run usability sessions and turn feedback into design changes.
Keep the Figma design system tidy, documented and up to date.

children.text: Optimize Your Talent Acquisition Funnel

Strong candidates rarely disappear at random. They drop out when job ads are vague, screening drags on for weeks, or nobody explains what happens next. Every lost applicant quietly costs your team time, budget and hiring momentum.

Our talent acquisition analysis maps your entire funnel, from the first job view to the signed offer. We measure conversion at every stage, compare your numbers with industry benchmarks, and show exactly where qualified people slip away and why it happens.
Our Service Deliverables

You receive a funnel audit with stage-by-stage conversion data, a sourcing channel scorecard, rewritten job ads for your top three roles, and a prioritized 90-day action plan that your recruiters and hiring managers can start on immediately.
Why Acquisition Data Matters

Hiring on instinct hides expensive problems. Clear data shows which channels bring hires who stay, which interview steps add no real value, and where one small change can lift your offer acceptance rate.
Key Benefits
Lower cost per hire
Faster time to fill
Stronger applicant quality
Clearer leadership reporting
Building Employer Brand Trust Through Hiring
Transparent salary ranges, honest role descriptions and timely updates turn applicants into advocates, even when they are not selected.

children.text: Optimize Your Onboarding Process

Many new hires decide whether to stay within their first few weeks. Missing equipment, unclear goals and busy managers leave them unsure where to start, and the excitement of accepting your offer quickly fades into doubt.

Our onboarding review examines every step from signed offer to the end of the first 90 days. We interview recent hires and managers, map where people feel lost, and design a clear, welcoming program that helps every newcomer settle in and contribute sooner.
Our Service Deliverables
You receive a preboarding checklist, a first-week schedule template, 30-60-90 day goal plans for key roles, a buddy program guide and a short new hire survey that tracks how each person settles in.
Why Onboarding Matters
Onboarding shapes how new employees feel about your company for years. A structured welcome builds confidence, speeds up productivity and makes people far more likely to stay beyond their first year.
Key Benefits
Faster time to productivity
Higher first-year retention
Stronger team connections
More confident managers
Building Belonging from Day One
Personal introductions, a dedicated buddy and regular check-ins help new hires feel part of the team before their first week ends.

children.text: Optimize Every Candidate Touchpoint

Applicants talk, and they compare notes. A slow reply, a broken application form or an interviewer who has not read the resume quickly becomes a public review that other candidates read before they ever decide to apply.

We walk through your hiring process exactly as a candidate would, interview recent applicants and new hires, and turn their honest feedback into a journey that feels clear, respectful and personal at every single step, from first click to first day.
Our Service Deliverables

The project delivers a complete candidate journey map, refreshed email and message templates, an interviewer briefing guide, and a short survey that measures candidate satisfaction after each stage so you can track progress over time.
Why Candidate Experience Matters

In a competitive market, the best people have options. A smooth, human process is often the deciding factor between two similar offers, and it protects your reputation with every applicant you decline.
Key Benefits
Higher offer acceptance
Fewer candidate drop-offs
Stronger online reviews
More applicant referrals
Building Trust Through Transparent Communication
Clear timelines, honest feedback and a named contact person show candidates you value their time, whether they join or not.

children.text: Optimize Your Retention Strategy

Replacing an experienced employee can cost up to a full year of their salary. Yet most companies only discover why people leave during the exit interview, when the decision is made and it is already far too late.

We analyze turnover data, engagement scores and exit feedback to find the real drivers behind resignations. Then we build a practical retention plan that targets the teams, managers and roles most at risk, with clear owners and measurable goals for each quarter.
Our Service Deliverables

You receive a retention risk dashboard, a recognition and reward framework, career path templates for your key roles, and a stay-interview guide that helps managers spot warning signs months before a valued employee starts looking elsewhere.
Why Employee Retention Matters

People who stay build knowledge, relationships and customer trust. Lower turnover means steadier teams, less pressure on recruiting, smoother handovers and more time for leaders to focus on growth instead of constant backfilling.
Key Benefits
Lower voluntary turnover
Higher engagement scores
Stronger internal mobility
Reduced replacement costs
Building Loyalty Through Clear Career Growth
Transparent promotion criteria, mentoring and regular development conversations show people their next step can happen inside your company.
